h1: The 8 Best Camera-Free Robot Vacuums of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Camera-Free Robot Vacuums: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 camera-free robot vacuums for privacy, scored on LiDAR, bump navigation and docks, from eufy to Roomba and roborock.
summary: The eufy Omni C20 is the best camera-free robot overall, combining vacuum and mop with a self-cleaning dock. The eufy C28 offers the most suction at 15,000 Pa, and the roborock Q7 M5+ stretches its dock to 7 to 9 weeks. The Roomba Max 705 brings obstacle sensors, while the Shark, Roomba 105 and eufy 11S MAX trade features for simplicity and price.
intro: The robot vacuums that get the most attention carry a front camera for object recognition. It spots cables and socks, and it also puts a lens in your bedroom. Plenty of buyers would rather skip that trade, and the good news is that the alternatives are not a step back in the way they used to be. LiDAR, a laser that measures distance, builds a floor plan with no image captured at all.

Every robot here navigates without an onboard camera, using LiDAR, bump sensors or cliff sensors. Our editors reviewed eight and ranked them on how well camera-free navigation suits a real home, then on suction, mopping and dock convenience. The Primea framework sets the scores, and bump-only robots drop where room size demands a map.

products.name: eufy Omni C20 Robot Vacuum and Mop Combo
products.verdict: Vacuum, mop and self-cleaning dock with no onboard camera. The most complete private option.
products.description:
The Omni C20 is the most complete camera-free machine in the group. It vacuums and mops, uses separate settings for hardwood and carpet, and steers with structural and cliff sensors instead of a lens. The self-cleaning dock handles mop upkeep, which is the chore robot owners abandon first.

It ranks above the C28 because the C20 packages the whole job, including washing its own mop, while the C28 has the higher suction. Compared with the roborock models, it adds the dock automation they lack, though they use LiDAR for mapping.

Buy it if you want privacy and minimal chores on a floor plan that mixes wood and carpet. The caveat is size: a large dock needs a real corner, and the machine sits in the $200 to $500 bucket.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest possible price.

products.name: eufy C28 Robot Vacuum and Mop Combo
products.verdict: 15,000 Pa and a spinning HydroJet roller mop. The camera-free scrubber.
products.description:
The C28 puts 15,000 Pa of suction, the highest figure in the ranking, behind a HydroJet roller mop. A spinning roller scrubs a floor rather than dragging a damp pad over it, which is a real difference on dried spills. A self-empty base cuts bin trips.

It ranks second because the C20's self-cleaning dock handles more upkeep, and the C28 does not wash its mop automatically. On carpet, however, the C28 is the stronger sweeper, since suction decides how deep it pulls.

Choose it for rugs, pets and heavy dirt in a camera-free robot. The caveat is the same price tier as the C20, in the $200 to $500 bucket, without the same level of dock automation. Check how you will clean the roller yourself.
cons: Less dock automation than the C20
products.idealFor: Rugs and heavy dirt, with privacy in mind.

products.name: roborock Q7 M5+ Robot Vacuum and Mop
products.verdict: LiDAR mapping, 10,000Pa and a dock rated up to 7 to 9 weeks. Camera-free and low maintenance.
products.description:
The Q7 M5+ uses LiDAR, not a camera, so it maps a floor plan from laser distance readings. Its 10,000 Pa suction and vacuum plus mop design are matched by a dock rated for up to 7 to 9 weeks before you swap the bag, a long gap for the class.

It ranks third because there is no self-washing mop, so the mop pad needs attention, and the eufy models above automate more. The Q10 S5+ shares its suction and navigation, but the Q7 adds the stated dock interval, which is the whole reason to choose it.

Buy it if you want mapped cleaning and the longest stretch between maintenance. The dock uses bags, so budget for replacements. Skip it if you want a washing mop, which the Omni C20 delivers.
products.idealFor: Mapped, low-maintenance cleaning with no camera.
products.skipIf: You want the mop washed automatically.

products.name: roborock Q10 S5+ Robot Vacuum and Mop
products.verdict: The same camera-free LiDAR as the Q7 at 10,000Pa. Strong on medium-pile carpet.
products.description:
The Q10 S5+ shares the Q7's camera-free LiDAR and 10,000 Pa suction, and it vacuums and mops. For medium-pile carpet and shedding pets, that suction rating is the number that matters, because it pulls fibre-trapped hair that weaker robots leave behind.

It ranks fourth, just below the Q7 M5+, because the two are nearly identical in features and the Q7 states a longer dock interval. The Q10 S5+ costs slightly less, which is the reason to pick it. The listing is thinner on dock detail, so confirm it before ordering.

Choose it for carpeted pet homes that want mapping without a lens. The caveat is that it offers nothing the Q7 lacks beyond price, and it does not wash its own mop.
cons: Close to the Q7 in features
products.idealFor: Carpeted pet homes wanting no camera.
products.skipIf: You want the longest dock interval.

products.name: iRobot Roomba Max 705 Robot Vacuum with AutoEmpty Dock
products.verdict: LiDAR plus obstacle and anti-fall sensors and dual rubber brushes, all without a camera.
products.description:
The Max 705 is the vacuum-only LiDAR option from iRobot. LiDAR plus obstacle and anti-fall sensors keep it off stairs and clear of walls with no camera, and dual rubber brushes resist the hair tangles that bristles collect. An AutoEmpty dock handles the bin.

It ranks fifth because it does not mop, while the roborock and eufy picks above all do. For a household where long hair and pet shedding are the enemy, the rubber brushes are the real draw, and the dock reduces how often you touch the bin.

Buy it for long-hair homes with mixed floors who do not need mopping. Dock bags will need replacing, so factor that in. If you want a mop, step up to the Q7 M5+ or the Omni C20.

products.name: Shark Navigator Robot Vacuum with Self-Empty Base RV2120AE
products.verdict: Bump and cliff sensors, a self-emptying dock and a brush that resists tangles.
products.description:
The Navigator steers by bump and cliff sensors, so it carries neither a lens nor a LiDAR turret. A self-empty base and a tangle-resistant brush roll aim it squarely at pet hair. For many homes that is enough, and it is the simplest docked option here.

It ranks sixth because bump navigation covers a floor by bouncing, not by planning neat rows. In a big home that wastes battery and time, and the LiDAR models finish faster. It also lacks mopping.

Buy it if you own a dog or cat, live in a modest space and want a docked vacuum with no cameras or mapping. The caveat is predictability: without a map, it cannot do no-go zones or targeted rooms, so it suits open layouts better than cluttered ones.
products.idealFor: Pet owners wanting a simple docked vacuum.

products.name: iRobot Roomba 105 Vac Robot Vacuum with LiDAR Navigation
products.verdict: LiDAR mapping and neat-row cleaning on a modest budget. No camera.
products.description:
The Roomba 105 is the cheapest way here to get LiDAR. It builds its map with a laser rather than a lens and sweeps in neat rows instead of a random bounce, which saves time on any floor plan. It charges itself.

It ranks seventh because the budget goes into navigation, so there is no dock and no mop. Against the Shark, which has a self-empty base but bump navigation, you trade bin convenience for smarter coverage. It sits in the $100 to $200 bucket, below the docked robots.

Buy it for a small to mid-sized home with hard floors where orderly vacuuming matters most. The caveat is that you empty the bin by hand after every run, and there is no mop at all.
products.skipIf: You need a dock or mopping.

products.name: eufy 11S MAX Robot Vacuum Cleaner
products.verdict: Slim, quiet and sensor-only. The cheapest guaranteed camera-free option.
products.description:
The 11S MAX is the simplest private robot here. A super thin profile slides under low furniture, bump and cliff sensors do the steering, and it runs quietly. With no camera and no mapping, it stores almost nothing about your home.

It ranks last on features, not on privacy. Random navigation takes longer to cover a floor than the LiDAR models, and it has neither a dock nor a mop. It also sits in the $100 to $200 bucket, so you are paying for simplicity.

Buy it for a small home with low furniture, and where a lens would never be acceptable. The caveat is coverage: it will miss patches in a large room, so expect to run it twice.
products.idealFor: Small homes wanting the simplest private robot.

whatMatters.detail: Camera-free means no lens captures images of your home. LiDAR spins a laser to measure distance and builds a map from those readings, while bump and cliff sensors detect contact and edges. All three avoid a camera. Look for the words LiDAR, bump sensors or no onboard camera in the listing before you assume a robot is camera-free.

Camera-based robots recognise cables and pet waste, while camera-free ones may drive over them. That is the main cost of privacy. Clear cables and socks before every run. A LiDAR robot with obstacle sensors, such as the Max 705, copes better than a bump-only model. Look for obstacle detection in the specs.

LiDAR plans neat rows and remembers rooms, while bump sensors bounce around and need more time. On a floor plan over about 1,000 square feet, LiDAR saves battery and finishes sooner, and it enables no-go zones. In one small room the difference is minor. Check the navigation line in the specifications rather than the title.

A robot without a camera can still send map data to the maker's cloud. If privacy is your real concern, read the app permissions and look for local control. Basic models such as the 11S MAX run from a button or remote, which avoids an account. Check the listing for app features and what registration requires.

Rubber brushes tangle less with long hair than bristles do. A camera-free robot cannot steer around hair clumps, so brush design matters more. The Max 705 uses dual rubber brushes, and the Shark lists a tangle-resistant roll. Look for anti-tangle or rubber brush in the specs, and plan to cut hair off any roller weekly.

faq.q: Do camera-free robot vacuums navigate worse?
faq.a: They can. Without a camera, a robot cannot recognise cables or socks, so it may bump or drive over them. LiDAR models such as the Roomba Max 705 still map well and add obstacle sensors to compensate.
No. LiDAR measures distance with a laser and builds a map from those readings, not images. The roborock Q7 M5+, Q10 S5+ and both Roombas here use LiDAR with no camera lens.

faq.q: Is the eufy Omni C20 worth the premium?
faq.a: If you want a hands-off mop, yes, because its dock washes the pad. If you only vacuum, the Roomba 105 or roborock Q10 S5+ cost less and map just as well using LiDAR.

faq.q: Will a bump-sensor robot damage furniture?
faq.a: Rarely. Bumpers are soft and light, so damage is uncommon. The eufy 11S MAX is slim and will tap furniture legs as it goes, but it will not harm solid pieces. Delicate items near the floor should be moved.

faq.q: Do I still need the app?
faq.a: For scheduling and maps, yes. Basic models like the eufy 11S MAX and Shark Navigator also run from a button or remote, so you can use them without sharing data with an account at all.

faq.q: How do I prepare my floors?
faq.a: Pick up cables, socks and pet bowls before each run, because there is no camera to avoid them. On LiDAR models such as the Q7 M5+ use no-go zones in the app for tricky areas.

finalTake: Buy the Omni C20 for a private, hands-off machine on mixed flooring, or the C28 when rugs and heavy dirt come first. LiDAR models such as the roborock Q7 M5+ suit larger homes. Choose the Roomba 105 or 11S MAX only if you accept limited extras, and always clear cables before a run.
